sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Start a company once there is revenue, and learn it
sections.para: Start a company as soon as there is revenue to put through it: it is professional, and companies, shares and their contracts have to be learned. The UK makes it cheap and simple; Portugal requires a paid accountant every month; Lithuania's e-residency is next.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Learn companies by doing; where you do it matters
sections.para: A company is a set of contracts a founder should understand and set. The UK takes an afternoon; Portugal is quick to form but costly to keep; Lithuania looks thought through. Count the cost as learning, and sell first.

sections.label: Why start a company
sections.line: A company makes you professional, and teaches you
sections.para: A company lets you register for things and keeps the work, money and intellectual property together. Above all, founders must learn balance sheets and shares. Start one when there is revenue; before that, register as a sole trader.

sections.label: A company is a set of contracts
sections.line: Read the contracts, and bring the rules yourself
sections.para: Large organisations have many companies, for liability and to segment the business. A company is governed by contracts that can favour founders or acquirers. Keep them simple and on your terms, and take investment only when profitable.

sections.label: The UK: the one I know well
sections.line: The UK: £100, a day, model articles by default
sections.para: Dinis's first UK company was formed at university so a client could pay. Today it is £100 online, usually within 24 hours, with model articles, a SIC code and identity checks. With no trade there is little to file; Corporation Tax starts with profit.

sections.label: Portugal: the one I learned the hard way
sections.line: Portugal: easy to form, costly by law to keep
sections.para: Empresa na Hora forms a company for €360. But every company must keep organised accounts signed by a certified accountant, trading or not. Dinis paid €200 to €300 a month for MyFeeds' company, and is closing it.

sections.label: Lithuania: the one I would like to go to next
sections.line: Lithuania: e-residency, and much still to find out
sections.para: E-residency, not e-citizenship: €90 for three years, a digital identity and signature. An MB needs no capital, a UAB €1,000, and a registered address. How much can be done remotely is unconfirmed; Dinis would like to find out by doing it.

sections.label: The cost of learning
sections.line: Spend money on learning, then sell
sections.para: The Portuguese company cost money, but money spent on learning is well spent. Start a company when you can trade, because what matters most is selling, experimenting and becoming profitable.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.para: Not legal or tax advice. The Portuguese cost is one experience in a published range; the legal requirement comes from two provisions read together; Lithuania is not decided; UK fees change.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: A memo, and the official sources
sections.para: Dinis's voice memo of 19 October 2026, checked against GOV.UK, Companies House, UK legislation, Portugal's justice and tax portals, the OCC statute, and Lithuanian sources, some secondary.
